clue.text: Jump on a plane for a quick getaway

parts.note: someone on a plane in the air is flying
to jump in alarm is to start

explanation.surface: Advice to catch a flight if you want to get away in a hurry.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come in answer order, so 'on a plane' goes first though 'Jump' is printed first. The setter also read it as a double definition; it is the '1 8' the airport clues point to.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking off in an aircraft literally starts you airborne, and in a race an advantage from the gun is the same idiom for an excellent beginning.

clue.text: Originally Killer Queen on reverse of single Edge of the Road

indicators.note: originally points to the opening letter of the word Killer, its beginning

parts.note: ER is Elizabeth Regina, the usual crossword abbreviation for the Queen
the flip side of a vinyl single record is called its B-side

explanation.surface: A rock-music trivia line about the Queen song 'Killer Queen' and its B-side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Killer Queen' is a Queen hit, so the surface reads as music trivia; 'on' is a link meaning 'placed beside', so K and ER sit before B-SIDE.
explanation.definitionFit: The kerb is the raised stone border of a pavement, so this word names the side of a street next to it.

clue.text: Go and get beers to be served in place of 18

indicators.note: drinks that are served are poured out and mixed, so these letters are shaken into a new order

explanation.surface: An invitation to go out for a few beers, in honour of a famous footballer who liked a drink.
explanation.walkthrough: '18' is the printed '1 8', FLYING START, so its place is an airport: Belfast's is George Best Belfast City Airport, named for the Northern Irish footballer. 'and' joins the two pieces of fodder, GO and GET BEERS.
explanation.definitionFit: Belfast City's airport is named after the footballer, so his name stands for a place where flights begin.

clue.text: Breast reduction essentially supported by virtuous character in place of 18

indicators.note: in a down clue the first piece sits on top of the second, which holds it up from below
a reduction of the word's essence, its middle, means one of its central letters is cut out

parts.note: boob is a slang word for a breast
hope is one of the three theological virtues, with faith and charity

explanation.surface: A cosmetic-surgery story about a breast reduction carried out on a virtuous patient.
explanation.walkthrough: BOOB loses one central O to give BOB, which stands above HOPE. '18' is the printed '1 8', FLYING START, so its place is an airport: Bob Hope Airport is in Burbank, California.
explanation.definitionFit: The Burbank airport in California carries the comedian's name, making it a spot where flights begin.

clue.text: Proust novel that'll send you to sleep

definitions.text: Proust novel that'll send you to sleep

indicators.note: novel as an adjective means new or fresh, so the letters of the author's name take a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A jibe that a novel by Proust is boring enough to put you to sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: 'novel' looks like the noun after Proust's name but works as an adjective meaning new, signalling the anagram; the whole clue is also the definition, a famously long book inducing a torpor.
explanation.definitionFit: A stupor is a heavy, dazed near-unconsciousness, the state a very long, dull read might leave you in.

clue.text: Damn! Rife roundabouts will make you Milton Keynes sceptic!

indicators.note: roundabouts send traffic circling, so these letters are turned around into a new order

explanation.surface: A complaint that Milton Keynes, a new town famous for its many roundabouts, is overrun with them.
explanation.walkthrough: Milton Keynes is an English new town notorious for its roundabouts; split the name and Milton Friedman, the monetarist economist, was a sceptic of John Maynard Keynes. He has an airport too, in Sacramento.
explanation.definitionFit: Milton Friedman, the Chicago economist, argued against Keynesian economics, so he was a doubter of Keynes.

Famous bell strikes the last time flanked by Royal Horse Artillery's cannon

indicators.note: to strike out is to delete, so the last letter of the bell's name is struck off

parts.note: Big Ben is the great bell in the clock tower of the Palace of Westminster

indicators.note: something flanked by others has them on both sides, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: RHA is the standard abbreviation for the Royal Horse Artillery

explanation.surface: Big Ben chimes the final hour while the Royal Horse Artillery fire a salute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strikes' suggests a bell chiming but means striking out the N of BIG BEN. Big Bertha was the German siege howitzer of the First World War.
explanation.definitionFit: Big Bertha was the nickname of a huge German howitzer, a heavy artillery gun of 1914.

clue.text: Stirring paean in Saint Paul's writings that'll make you catch your breath?

definitions.text: in Saint Paul's writings that'll make you catch your breath?

indicators.note: stirring mixes something up, so the letters of the hymn of praise are churned into a new order

explanation.surface: A rousing hymn in the epistles of Saint Paul that leaves you breathless.
explanation.walkthrough: The British spelling is APNOEA; Saint Paul here is the city in Minnesota, so the definition asks for the American spelling. 'Stirring' looks like an adjective praising the paean but signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Apnoea is a temporary halt in breathing, as in sleep apnoea, and an American writer drops the O.

clue.text: Imagine his output in location of 18

explanation.surface: A tribute to the man who wrote 'Imagine', now an airport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Imagine' was this Beatle's best-known solo song. '18' is the printed '1 8', FLYING START, so its location is an airport: Liverpool's is Liverpool John Lennon Airport.
explanation.definitionFit: The ex-Beatle wrote and recorded the song 'Imagine', and Liverpool renamed its airport after him in 2001.

clue.text: Kindle Fire in amongst foreign items

indicators.note: in amongst says the letters sit inside a run of the clue words that follow

explanation.surface: Amazon's Kindle Fire tablet found among items brought from abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: The Kindle Fire is Amazon's tablet, but here the two words are verbs, each meaning to set alight.
explanation.definitionFit: To kindle a fire is to start it burning, to set something alight.

clue.text: Model covered by bikini top in trailers for Home and Away?

indicators.note: one letter covered by another is hidden under it, replaced by it in the word

parts.note: trailers are advertisements for coming programmes or films
the Model T was Henry Ford's famous car, so model gives the letter T

indicators.note: the first letter of the word it picks from

parts.note: the top of the word bikini is its first letter, b

explanation.surface: A glamour model in a bikini top appears in promos for the Australian soap 'Home and Away'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home and Away' is an Australian TV soap, so trailers seem apt; but home and away are both adverbs ('go home', 'run away'), hence the question mark. 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Words like home and away modify verbs, telling where an action happens, which makes them examples of that part of speech.

clue.text: Out of The Sun? Receiving The Times for a period

indicators.note: in a down entry the first piece receives the second, which arrives beneath it

parts.note: a place out of the sun is shady and dark
ages means times or eras

explanation.surface: Someone who stopped reading The Sun and took The Times for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun and The Times are British newspapers, which the capitals push; here they are plain words. The Dark Ages is the early medieval period in Europe.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dark Ages is the name for the early medieval era after Rome fell, a span of history.

clue.text: See 3
Mo Farah's second going into home straight — triumphing initially by not losing heart

indicators.note: one piece going into another is placed inside it

parts.note: in means at home

indicators.note: initially takes the opening letter of each of the two words straight and triumphing
losing its heart means the word not drops its middle letter
second picks out the letter in position two of the athlete's surname

explanation.surface: Mo Farah's racing commentary: entering the home straight, winning narrowly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mo Farah' reads as the runner, but 'Mo' alone is the definition, a moment, and 'Farah's second' gives A. 'by' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A mo is British slang for a moment, as in 'wait a mo', and that tiny span is a moment too.

clue.text: Chado?

parts.note: chado is the Japanese tea ceremony; split as CHA plus DO it also reads as a word for tea followed by a word for a social gathering

explanation.walkthrough: CHA is slang for tea and DO is a party, so the clue's one word splits into the answer's two halves; the question mark marks this second reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Chado is the Japanese ceremony of serving tea, a formal social occasion built around the drink.

explanation.walkthrough: 'Loose Women' is a British daytime TV chat show, which the capitals point to, but here it means promiscuous women. 'with' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A floosie is an old-fashioned disparaging word for a woman of easy morals, so she is one of the promiscuous women.
